items.followUp: Why does ice have a lower density than liquid water?

rubric.why: Explains the structure responsible for ice’s lower density.
rubric.description: Ice forms an open structure because of hydrogen bonding.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking hydrogen bonding to an open or expanded structure in ice.

rubric.why: States the density difference that makes ice float.
rubric.description: The open structure makes ice less dense than liquid water, so it floats.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that ice is less dense than water or that this causes it to float.

modelAnswer: Hydrogen bonds arrange water molecules in ice into an open, expanded structure.
This makes ice less dense than liquid water, so it floats on water.

items.followUp: Why does an ice cube float in a glass of water?

rubric.why: Dynamic equilibrium requires the opposing reactions to continue at equal rates.
rubric.description: The forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that both reactions continue and their rates are equal.

rubric.why: Equal opposing rates produce no overall change in the system.
rubric.description: The concentrations of reactants and products remain constant.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that concentrations remain constant or there is no overall change.

modelAnswer: Dynamic equilibrium is the state in a reversible reaction in which the forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates.
As a result, the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant.

items.followUp: What keeps the particles of a colloid from settling out quickly?

rubric.why: Identifies the small size and persistent dispersion of colloidal particles.
rubric.description: Colloidal particles are very small and remain dispersed rather than settling under gravity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the particles are small and do not settle.

rubric.why: Gives a reason the particles remain dispersed.
rubric.description: Their continuous Brownian motion, or mutual repulsion due to like charges, helps keep them dispersed.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for Brownian motion or repulsion between similarly charged particles.

modelAnswer: Colloidal particles are very small and remain dispersed instead of settling under gravity.
Their continuous Brownian motion, and often repulsion between like charges, helps keep the colloid stable.

items.followUp: How does metallic character change down a group and across a period?

rubric.why: Tests the group trend in electropositivity.
rubric.description: Electropositivity increases down a group.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct down-group trend.

rubric.why: Tests the period trend in electropositivity.
rubric.description: Electropositivity decreases from left to right across a period.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct left-to-right period trend.

modelAnswer: Electropositivity increases down a group.
It decreases from left to right across a period.

items.followUp: Give five differences between an element and a compound.

rubric.why: Contrasts how compounds are formed and their fixed composition.
rubric.description: A compound contains elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio; a mixture has substances physically combined in variable proportions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the contrast between chemical combination/fixed ratio and physical mixing/variable proportions.

rubric.why: Contrasts the properties of a compound with those of its components in a mixture.
rubric.description: A compound has properties different from its elements; substances in a mixture retain their own properties.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this property contrast.

rubric.why: Contrasts the methods needed to separate the substances.
rubric.description: Elements in a compound can be separated by chemical methods; components of a mixture can be separated by physical methods.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly contrasting chemical separation from physical separation.

rubric.why: Identifies characteristic fixed points of compounds.
rubric.description: A compound has definite melting and boiling points, unlike a mixture, which generally has a range.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the fixed points of compounds or the range for mixtures.

rubric.why: Contrasts the uniform composition of a compound with the possible variation in a mixture.
rubric.description: A compound is homogeneous, whereas a mixture may be homogeneous or heterogeneous.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this contrast.

modelAnswer: A compound contains elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio; a mixture contains substances physically mixed in variable proportions.
A compound has properties different from its constituent elements; the substances in a mixture retain their own properties.
The elements of a compound are separated by chemical methods; mixture components can be separated by physical methods.
A pure compound has definite melting and boiling points; a mixture generally melts or boils over a range.
A compound is homogeneous; a mixture may be homogeneous or heterogeneous.

items.followUp: Write four properties of cathode rays.

rubric.why: Identifies the charge or nature of canal rays.
rubric.description: Canal rays consist of positively charged particles (positive ions).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying them as positively charged ions.

rubric.why: Tests their path of travel.
rubric.description: They travel in straight lines.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that canal rays travel in straight lines.

rubric.why: Tests their behaviour in fields or relative to cathode rays.
rubric.description: They are deflected by electric and magnetic fields, in the direction expected for positive charge (opposite to cathode rays).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct field-deflection property or the correct contrast with cathode rays.

rubric.why: Tests the dependence of canal-ray particles on the gas used.
rubric.description: Their particles and mass-to-charge ratio depend on the gas in the discharge tube.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the particles or their mass-to-charge ratio depend on the gas.

modelAnswer: Canal rays consist of positively charged particles, or positive ions.
They travel in straight lines.
They are deflected by electric and magnetic fields in the direction expected for positive charges, opposite to cathode rays.
Their particles, and their mass-to-charge ratio, depend on the gas present in the discharge tube.

items.followUp: Describe single, double and triple covalent bonds, giving one example of each.

rubric.why: Defines a single covalent bond by the number of shared electron pairs.
rubric.description: A single covalent bond is formed by sharing one pair of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one shared pair.

rubric.why: Provides a valid example of a single covalent bond.
rubric.description: Hydrogen molecule (H₂) is an example of a single covalent bond.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct single-bond example.

rubric.why: Defines a double covalent bond by the number of shared electron pairs.
rubric.description: A double covalent bond is formed by sharing two pairs of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for two shared pairs.

rubric.why: Defines a triple bond or gives its standard example.
rubric.description: A triple covalent bond is formed by sharing three pairs of electrons; nitrogen molecule (N₂) is an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for three shared pairs or a correct triple-bond example.

modelAnswer: A covalent bond is formed when atoms share electron pairs.
A single covalent bond has one shared pair; for example, H₂.
A double covalent bond has two shared pairs; for example, O₂.
A triple covalent bond has three shared pairs; for example, N₂.

items.followUp: Define an unsaturated solution and describe how to prepare one.

rubric.why: Recognizes that saturation is defined for a particular temperature.
rubric.description: A saturated solution is defined at a specified temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning the temperature condition.

rubric.why: States the defining maximum-solute condition.
rubric.description: It contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at that temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the maximum-solute definition.

rubric.why: Gives the first practical preparation step.
rubric.description: Add the solute gradually to a measured amount of solvent.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for gradual addition of solute.

rubric.why: Explains how to tell when the solution has become saturated.
rubric.description: Stir until no more solute dissolves; some excess solid may remain undissolved.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stirring until no more dissolves or noting excess undissolved solute.

modelAnswer: A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a specified temperature.
Measure the solvent and add the solute gradually while stirring.
Continue until no more solute dissolves; any excess remains undissolved.
The solution is then saturated at that temperature.
